procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached by the Appellants (presumably the accused in the FIR). The Supreme Court stayed further proceedings qua the appellants on 30.10.2015. The Supreme Court was considering whether the High Court has the power to quash an FIR under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure even when a chargesheet has been filed during the pendency of the petition to quash the FIR.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, to quash an FIR when a chargesheet has been filed by the police during the pendency of the quash petition.

facts: A petition was filed in the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) seeking to quash a First Information Report (FIR).
While this quash petition was pending before the High Court, the police completed their investigation and filed a chargesheet in the matter.
law: Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. grants the High Court inherent power to make such orders as may be necessary to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

The Supreme Court cited its previous judgments in *Joseph Salvaraj A. vs. State of Gujarat* (2011) and *Anand Kumar Mohatta and another vs. State (NCT of Delhi)* (2019) as established precedents on this issue.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the quash petition against the FIR should be dismissed simply because a chargesheet had been filed.

The Court affirmed that it is a "well settled" principle that the High Court's power to entertain and act upon a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is not extinguished by the subsequent filing of a chargesheet during the pendency of the petition.
The Court stated that this principle has been previously established and reiterated in prior cases, and therefore, the issue required no further detailed explanation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the High Court continues to have the power under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to entertain a petition and quash an FIR, even when a chargesheet is filed by the police during the pendency of that petition.

issue.issue_text: Whether the FIR and the criminal case pending against the appellants under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code and Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, should be quashed.

facts: The appellants are the mother-in-law and two brothers-in-law of the complainant (wife).
The wife filed a complaint alleging mental and physical harassment for dowry under Section 498A IPC and the Dowry Prohibition Act.
The complaint was filed four years after the wife had left her matrimonial home, and only after her husband had instituted divorce proceedings.
The court found the allegations to be mostly general and omnibus in nature, lacking specific details about how and when the harassment occurred.
The appellants (in-laws) lived in different cities from the complainant and her husband.
law: The High Court has the inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) to quash an FIR and consequential proceedings to prevent the abuse of the process of law or to secure the ends of justice.
This power to quash an FIR under Section 482 Cr.P.C. remains with the High Court even if a chargesheet is filed by the police while the quash petition is pending.
application: The Court found the allegations to be "wholly insufficient" and, prima facie, not making out a case against the appellants.
The allegations were deemed "so farfetched and improbable that no prudent person can conclude that there are sufficient grounds to proceed against them."

The Court noted "glaring inconsistencies and discrepancies," particularly the four-year delay in filing the complaint, which suggested that the wife's motives were not clean and that she wanted to "wreak vengeance."

Given the vague nature of the allegations and the fact that the in-laws lived elsewhere, the Court concluded that permitting the criminal process to continue would result in a "clear and patent injustice."
The Court held that this was a fit case where the High Court should have exercised its inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appeal and quashed the FIR and the criminal case pending against the appellants (the mother-in-law and two brothers-in-law).

cases.case_name: State of Haryana and others vs. Bhajan Lal and others
cases.principle: To set out, by way of illustration, the broad categories of cases in which the inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. could be exercised to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be exercised to quash criminal proceedings where the allegations in an FIR or complaint are so insufficient, farfetched, or improbable that they do not disclose the commission of any offense, and no prudent person could conclude that there are sufficient grounds to proceed against the accused. This power may also be exercised where there is an express legal bar to the institution and continuance of the proceedings under the relevant code or act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the allegations against the appellants (the in-laws) were wholly insufficient and did not prima facie make out a case against them. The allegations were deemed so far-fetched and improbable that no prudent person could conclude there were sufficient grounds to proceed. The case was determined to fall squarely within categories (1) and (5) of the principles laid down in the State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal case, making it a fit case for the High Court to have exercised its inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the FIR and consequential proceedings.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the illustrative categories from State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal for exercising inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, specifically:

Category (1): Where the allegations made in the ﬁrst information report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any oﬀence or make out a case against the accused.

Category (5): Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is suﬃcient ground for proceeding against the accused.
policy_considerations: Permitting the criminal process to go on against the appellants in such a situation would result in clear and patent injustice.
The inherent power under Section 482 of the Code should be exercised to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.
